stem_text: Sand is being dropped from a stationary dropper at a rate of 0.5kgs^(−1) on a conveyor belt moving with a velocity of 5ms^(−1) . The power needed to keep the belt moving with the same velocity will be :

candidate_solve.assumed_parameters_from_coaching_figure: None required (pure text). Sand dropped from rest vertically.
candidate_solve.derivation: Mass rate dm/dt = 0.5 kg/s, belt velocity v = 5 m/s. The horizontal force required to accelerate newly dropped sand to belt speed is F = v * (dm/dt) = 5 m/s * 0.5 kg/s = 2.5 N. The power supplied by the motor to maintain constant velocity is P = F * v = 2.5 N * 5 m/s = 12.5 W.
candidate_solve.limiting_cases: Rate of gain of kinetic energy of sand is d(KE)/dt = 1/2 (dm/dt) v^2 = 1/2 (0.5)(25) = 6.25 W. An equal amount of power (6.25 W) is dissipated as heat in friction as the sand slips on the belt. Total power input by the motor must be 6.25 + 6.25 = 12.5 W.

sl2.crux: Applying variable-mass force relation F = v(dm/dt) to calculate required external motor power P = F*v = v^2(dm/dt), recognizing that mechanical power is twice the rate of kinetic energy increase.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Variable-mass mechanics applied to steady conveyor belt.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Force from mass flow -> power from F*v.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Severe attractor trap: computing d(1/2 m v^2)/dt = 6.25 W (Option C) by ignoring frictional heat dissipation.

wrong_route_hypotheses.route: Calculating pure rate of KE gain d(KE)/dt = 1/2 v^2 dm/dt = 6.25 W (Option C)
Dividing force by velocity instead of multiplying: 2.5 / 5 = 0.5 W
